chapter: Bix's methods and New Orleans musicians
title: Bix at the piano; Trumbauer's role
summary: Discussion of Bix's piano recordings and Trumbauer's neglected contribution.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Well, where, where did, did Bix, could Bix play those kind of chords in the Whiteman Orchestra? I mean, was he able to work that out there?
Well, no, well, you see, the thing is, what you must remember is that he wasn't playing piano with the Whiteman Orchestra. Right, right. He was playing trumpet in the orchestra.
He didn't play any piano with any groups, did he?
The only, I don't remember, the only thing he played piano that I can remember is when he recorded with the trio and trombone. Big Boy. Huh?
He plays piano on Big Boy with the Wolverines.
With the Wolverines? Yeah, I think, you know, I think that's a... Yeah, one piece. I don't remember. Maybe, yeah. No, I don't remember that. I never, I never remember that. He might, yeah.

Those three were featured within the band. Incidentally, I think it's Singing the Blues by Trombauer. It lists Bix, Tram, and Lange. It lists those three. Bix, Tram, and Lange, yeah. Yeah. You know? Yeah, and it's interesting that the company knew enough to do that then. The record companies knew that, you know, they weren't dumb.
And he goes from the piano to the cornet right at the end. He plays the piano. Yeah, on both sides, huh? Yeah, and then he switches to the cornet at the end for a brief... Yeah.
Well, he used to do that, yeah, he did that quite a lot. But he didn't do that while he was playing with White.
But Trombauer seemed to be the one who was most sympathetic to that kind of chord progression and things like that.

That's why I say I really think that Trombauer was really such a great man with him. I don't know. I think he's very neglected. Very neglected. I'd say he almost fit in a category with Bix because everything they did, they did together, you know? Yeah. Everything. I'm sure there was many ideas that Trombauer gave that helped Bix. Maybe we might say this. Maybe he didn't tell him what to play on, singing the blues or anything like that. But his inspiration, you know, would... Because I've played with musicians that have inspired me. That led me on to do things that I never thought that I could do. This can't happen to you. That's one of the great things that I liked about New Orleans. Even so, even just as you said something about this, something similar to this in the conversation here, that I wanted to bring that point out, was that knowing the musicians meant so much in New Orleans here. Because each man that you knew had such individuality. And I mean, just to be around these people... Except for Monk. They would do something for you, you know? Even the Sharky. Sharky, who everybody said, oh, he's the greatest trumpet player. He's the greatest New Orleans jazz trumpet player that they ever had. He played Dixieland music. He really played good New Orleans music. He had a good style. He only had a different disposition, you know? But even with his disposition, I loved him. I thought he was tremendous, you know? And I think this was a part of all New Orleans musicians. Even to Papa Lane. I mean, he was a great old guy.
